fetched_contents.text: Sebaceous carcinoma of the chest wall: A case report Abstract Sebaceous carcinoma is a rare, malignant tumor of the sebaceous glands. This is a case report of a 75-year-old man who presented with a right lower axillary mass which initially was considered to be a benign sebaceous cyst from sonography. The lesion rapidly changed in clinical and sonographic appearances and on histology was a sebaceous carcinoma. This unusual tumor accounts for less than 1% of all cutaneous malignant tumors, and the chest wall is a rare extraocular site with only nine cases described in the literature. Immunohistochemistry was negative for MSH2 and MSH6, and positive for MLH1 and PMS2, raising the possibility of Lynch or Muir-Torre Syndrome which is a known association with this rare tumor. Introduction Sebaceous carcinomas (SC) is a rare but aggressive tumor of the sebaceous glands, accounting for less than 1% of all cutaneous malignant tumors. Although SC can arise from a sebaceous gland within any part of the skin, these are usually confined to the eyelid with extra-ocular presentations in only one quarter of reported cases. Moreover, there are only 9 reported cases of axillary presentation of SC and in these circumstances a diagnosis of Muir-Torre syndrome should be considered in patients diagnosed with a primary SC. [1–2] Furthermore, surgical excision is the recommended primary treatment modality and this includes Moh's micrographic surgery [3]. An unusual case of SC is presented with accompanying imaging that is crucial for differential diagnosis of this entity. Recognition of suspicious clinical and radiological features that are not typical of a benign epidermoid cyst is pertinent for making a correct diagnosis. Case report A 75-year-old man presented to his general practitioner with a 3-month history of a painless lump in the right axilla. Examination revealed a discrete 3 cm soft mass within the skin of the chest wall in the mid-axillary line. There was some red discoloration of the overlying skin but no punctum and no signs of acute inflammation. There was no ipsilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. The differential diagnosis was between a sebaceous cyst or lipoma and an ultrasound examination was requested by the general practitioner. This showed a well-defined but heterogeneous mass in the skin measuring 10 × 13 mm with peripheral and central vascularization on color Doppler scanning (Fig. 1). As the lesion lay within the skin and had clinical features consistent with a sebaceous cyst, this was the presumed diagnosis. Nonetheless, on account of enhanced vascularity of the lesion on imaging, further radiological opinion was sought; the degree of vascularity was not considered typical of a benign sebaceous cyst and repeat sonographic assessment was arranged and undertaken after a COVID-19 related delay of 12 weeks. This revealed an increase in size of the mass that now measured 21 × 15 mm and displayed lobulations with marked internal vascularity on Doppler. Moreover, the lesion encroached into the subcutaneous tissues but no axillary lymphadenopathy was seen. These appearances were concerning for a malignant lesion either of primary origin or a secondary deposit. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy was undertaken with a 16 G needle and 3 passes (Fig. 2). The patient was subsequently referred for urgent assessment in the Cambridge Breast Unit where further enquiry revealed the patient to be otherwise well with no evidence of weight loss, back pain or cough and no history of previous skin cancer. He was a non-smoker with minimal alcohol intake and had non-insulin dependent diabetes mellitus. On further examination, there was a hard, irregular but mobile mass lying in the skin and subcutaneous tissues of the lateral chest wall in the region of the low axilla. This measured 3 cm in maximum diameter and was clinically suspicious with incipient ulceration of the overlying skin (Fig. 2). There was no axillary lymphadenopathy nor other chest wall lesions. The case was reviewed at the breast multidisciplinary team meeting and histology revealed a malignant tumor comprised of sheets of basaloid cells with zones of overt sebaceous gland differentiation. There was prominent mitotic activity along with some apoptotic debris and moderate cellular pleomorphism within the basaloid cells. The sebaceous cells were seen to merge into squamous epithelium with keratinization and giant cells with fibrosis were present in the adjacent connective tissue. These features were consistent with a sebaceous carcinoma that was confirmed on subsequent immunohistochemistry (negative staining for MSH2 and MSH6 and positive staining for MLH1 and PMS2). This immune-profile also raised the possibility of Lynch or Muir-Torre syndromes. A contrast-enhanced CT staging scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis revealed no evidence of regional nodal nor distant metastatic disease. The patient was referred to the skin and plastics multidisciplinary teams for further management of this rare cutaneous malignancy. It was recommended the lesion be excised widely with a minimum surgical margin of clearance of 10 mm and ideally 20 mm. The location of the lesion permitted primary closure without excessive mobilization of tissues. No axillary surgical staging procedure was undertaken due to normality of nodes on imaging with both ultrasound and CT scan, but regular clinical follow up with an initial interval CT scan was arranged (Fig. 3). fetched_contents.text: Alternative cancer treatments: 11 options to consider Talk to your healthcare professional if you're interested in trying any of these integrative treatments. Accupuncture. During acupuncture treatment, an acupuncture specialist inserts tiny needles into your skin at precise points. Studies show acupuncture may be helpful in improving sleep and reducing nausea caused by chemotherapy. Acupuncture also may help relieve certain types of pain in people with cancer. It may help with hot flashes in those with breast cancer who are taking medicines that may affect hormone levels. Acupuncture is usually safe if it's performed by a trained professional using sterile needles. Ask your healthcare professional for names of trusted professionals. Acupuncture isn't always safe if you're taking blood thinners or if you have low blood counts, so check with your healthcare team first. Acupressure is a related technique in which mild pressure is applied to certain areas, such as the wrist, to help relieve nausea. Aromatherapy. Aromatherapy uses fragrant oils to provide a calming sensation. Oils infused with scents such as lavender can be applied to your skin during a massage. You also can add the oils to bath water. Fragrant oils can be heated to release their scents into the air. Aromatherapy may be helpful in relieving nausea. While there are trained professionals who offer aromatherapy, you also may use aromatherapy on your own. Aromatherapy is safe, although oils applied to the skin can cause allergic reactions. People with cancer that is sensitive to the effects of estrogen, such as some breast cancers, may want to avoid applying large amounts of lavender oil or tea tree oil to the skin. These oils may have effects similar to hormones if you apply too much. Exercise. Exercise may help you manage symptoms during and after cancer treatment. Gentle exercise may help relieve fatigue and stress and help you sleep better. Many studies show that an exercise program may help people with cancer live longer and improve their overall quality of life. If you haven't been exercising often, check with your healthcare team before you begin an exercise program. Specialists in physical therapy and occupational therapy and lymphedema therapists can assess your needs and make a safe plan. Start slowly, adding more exercise as you go. Branch report: diagnosis and likely causes of the back lump

The most common benign causes of a back lump are lipomas, sebaceous cysts, and other soft-tissue masses, with the evidence here emphasizing that lipomas must be differentiated from other masses or tumors, including sebaceous cysts or abscesses [N1-R5]. A sebaceous cyst is a benign, fluid-filled growth that can be confused with a lipoma, and the literature explicitly states that a sebaceous carcinoma can be mistaken for a benign sebaceous cyst [N1-F1]. In addition, a general cancer-oriented source notes that persistent lumps or swelling in any part of the body should be taken seriously, including lumps in the chest or back [N2-F2]. The AFP article on soft-tissue masses also says that benign and malignant masses can be painless, but those that present suddenly without explanation or are firm, deep, and adhere to surrounding structures are more worrisome [N1-R3].

Red flags that suggest cancer or serious pathology include rapid growth, change in appearance, hardness, fixation to surrounding tissue, and features that do not match the usual benign picture. In the case report of sebaceous carcinoma, the lesion was initially considered a benign sebaceous cyst, but the patient’s mass changed in clinical and sonographic appearance, became larger, and showed increased vascularity and lobulations, which were concerning for a malignant lesion [N1-F1]. Another source explicitly notes that a new lump should be professionally evaluated because most lumps are benign, but any new lump should be taken seriously [N2-F2]. The NHS cancer page also lists a new lump or swelling as a possible symptom of cancer, alongside other red flags such as sweating, weight loss, and unusual bruising or bleeding [N2-F2]. The urgent evaluation guidance further states that hard, fixed lumps larger than 1 inch, rapidly growing lumps, and noticeable enlargement are urgent signs that warrant urgent evaluation within 1–3 days [N2-R3].

When imaging or biopsy is needed, the evidence supports an expedited imaging approach if the mass is worrisome. The AFP article recommends initial radiography followed by an expedited MRI with contrast, pending radiology recommendation and referral to a specialist [N4-R3]. The case report itself shows that ultrasound was used initially, but the appearance of increased vascularity and size prompted further radiological opinion and eventual core biopsy [N1-F1]. The oncologic imaging guideline also notes that patients with persistent disease may be managed with close follow-up for up to 6 months, but this is a management recommendation rather than a diagnostic first step [N4-R2]. In short, the safest approach is to refer a suspicious lump to dermatology or oncology promptly and to use imaging or biopsy if the mass appears malignant or indeterminate [N1-F1][N4-R3].

Overall, the evidence supports a diagnosis-first approach: most back lumps are benign, but a suspicious lump should not be ignored because it may represent a rare but serious condition like sebaceous carcinoma [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## Final integrated answer to the patient

You’re not alone in feeling worried about a lump on your back. This is a common concern, and the good news is that most lumps are not cancer, but it is important to take this seriously because some serious conditions can mimic a benign growth.

---

## 1) What the lump could be

The evidence suggests that the most common **benign causes** of a back lump are **lipomas** and **sebaceous cysts**, with other soft-tissue masses also possible [N1-R5][N1-R3]. A **sebaceous cyst** is a benign, fluid-filled lump, while a **lipoma** is a fatty lump that is usually soft and movable [N1-R5]. However, the same evidence also warns that **sebaceous carcinoma** — a rare but aggressive skin cancer — can be mistaken for a benign sebaceous cyst [N1-F1]. That is why a lump should not be dismissed simply because it feels harmless.

### Red flags that may suggest something more serious
There are several signs that should prompt concern:
- The lump is **growing rapidly** or changing in appearance [N2-F2][N1-F1]
- It is **hard, fixed, or adherent to surrounding tissue** [N1-R3]
- It is **larger than 1 inch** or feels **noticeably enlarged** [N2-R3]
- It has features that **do not match the usual benign picture**, such as increased vascularity, lobulations, or skin changes [N1-F1]
- It is accompanied by other **warning signs of cancer**, such as unexplained weight loss, fatigue, or unusual bruising or bleeding [N2-F2]

The evidence also notes that many red flags have **high false positive rates**, so a single suspicious feature does **not** automatically mean cancer [N2-R1]. But that does not mean you should ignore the warning.

---

## 2) When imaging or biopsy is needed

If a lump is worrisome, the evidence supports an **expedited imaging approach** rather than waiting. The AFP guidance says that when a worrisome mass is found, initial radiography followed by an expedited MRI with contrast is recommended [N4-R3]. In the case report of sebaceous carcinoma, ultrasound was used initially, but the suspicious appearance of increased vascularity and size prompted further radiological opinion and eventually a core biopsy [N1-F1].

So the practical rule is:
- **See a specialist** quickly if the lump is growing, changing, hard, or concerning
- **Imaging** is often needed to better define the lump
- **Biopsy or specialist referral** is needed if the mass looks malignant or indeterminate

This is not a suggestion to rush into surgery, but rather to get the right diagnosis as soon as possible.

---

## 3) Natural remedies and “cancer fixes” — what to know

You asked about a “natural fix,” and that is a very important point.

### What is supported by evidence
The evidence supports **acupuncture** as one of the few complementary approaches with a credible role in symptom management. It may help with:
- **nausea and vomiting** related to cancer treatment
- **pain**
- **sleep problems**
- **fatigue**
- **hot flashes in breast cancer**
- **quality of life improvements** [N3-R5][N6-R5][N6-R3][N6-R4]

These are **symptom-management benefits**, not a cure for a lump or tumor. That is important: acupuncture is **not** a substitute for medical evaluation.

### What is not supported or may be harmful
The evidence is clear that **many natural remedies are unsupported by strong evidence** and should be regarded with caution [N5-R2][N5-F4]. The NCI CAM page explains that **CAM therapies are used outside standard medical care**, and most complementary therapies still need more research to prove helpful [N5-F4]. It also notes that **alternative therapies** are used **instead of** standard treatment, which is a red flag [N5-F4].

The MSKCC article reinforces this by stating that “natural” cancer therapies should be regarded with **great caution** because most are **unsupported by evidence** [N5-R2]. It also highlights that people often offer testimonials to these therapies despite the lack of scientific support [N5-R2].

### How to distinguish plausible from dangerous claims
- **Plausible** claims are those that are **not inherently harmful** and have **some evidence of safety or benefit** in a limited context, such as acupuncture for nausea or pain [N3-R5][N6-R4]
- **Dangerous** claims are those that:
  - promise to **cure cancer**
  - claim to **eliminate tumors**
  - use **unsupported “natural” language** to imply a cure or replacement for medical care
  - are **not backed by strong evidence** [N5-R2][N5-F4]

In short, the best evidence supports **acupuncture for symptom management**, while most natural “cures” are **unsupported and should not be used as substitutes for medical evaluation** [N5-R2][N3-R5].

---

## 4) Evidence-based supportive care and patient safety

If you are concerned about symptom management, the evidence supports a few **safe, evidence-based options**:
- **Acupuncture** for nausea, pain, sleep, fatigue, and quality of life [N3-R5][N6-R5][N6-R4]
- **Exercise** as a safe way to manage fatigue and improve quality of life [N3-F3]
- **Relaxation techniques, meditation, and mindfulness** for anxiety and stress [N5-F4]

The NCI CAM page also notes that some complementary practices may be **safe if used appropriately** and that people should discuss CAM use with their healthcare provider before trying them [N5-F4]. That is the key message: do **not** self-treat with unproven remedies.

### Safety concerns for non-medical self-care
The evidence is clear that many natural remedies are **not supported by strong evidence** and may be **harmful if used as alternatives to standard care** [N5-R2][N5-F4]. 5. **Discuss any complementary therapies** with your healthcare provider before using them [N5-F4]
6. **Use evidence-based supportive care** only if recommended by a provider, such as acupuncture for nausea or fatigue [N3-R5][N6-R4]

---

## 7) How to communicate uncertainty and urgency

A good way to explain this to a patient is:
- “Most lumps are benign, but this one should not be ignored because some serious conditions can look like a harmless lump.”
- “The lump should be evaluated promptly because it may be growing, changing, or having features that suggest something more serious.”
- “I do not want to alarm you, but we should not wait if there is any sign that this might not be a simple cyst.”
- “If you try any natural remedies, please talk to your doctor first. Some things may be helpful, but many are not supported by evidence.”

This approach is honest, reassuring, and medically appropriate.

---

## Bottom line

- **Likely causes:** lipoma, sebaceous cyst, and rare but serious possibilities such as sebaceous carcinoma [N1-R5][N1-F1]
- **Red flags:** rapid growth, change, hardness, fixation, size, and other cancer warning signs [N2-F2][N2-R3][N1-F1]
- **Next steps:** see a doctor quickly, get imaging or biopsy if needed, and avoid delaying care [N4-R3][N2-F2]
- **Natural remedies:** acupuncture is the only evidence-supported complementary approach; most natural “cures” are unsupported and should not replace medical evaluation [N5-R2][N3-R5][N5-F4]
- **Safety:** do not rely on unproven self-care; discuss any complementary therapy with your provider [N5-F4]
- **Urgency:** waiting may be dangerous because some serious conditions can develop or change quickly [N1-F1][N2-F2]
